Offences Against the Person Act 1861. That section, as amended in 2008, provides:

(1) A person is guilty of an offence if he or she intentionally causes or attempts to cause grievous bodily harm.

(2) A person is guilty of an offence if he or she, without lawful authority or excuse, assaults another, so as to cause or attempt to cause grievous bodily harm.

(3) A person is guilty of an offence if he or she, without lawful authority or excuse, has a firearm, explosive or offensive weapon in his or her custody or control in public or on any private premises with the intention of using it or attempting to use it to commit an offence under this section.

(4) A person guilty of an offence under this section is liable—

(a) on conviction on indictment, to imprisonment for life;

(b) on summary conviction, to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 5 years.

As I have stated, the purpose of this Bill is to increase the maximum penalties for these offences. It does this by inserting a new section 26A in the 1861 Act, which provides:

A person guilty of an offence under section 26 is liable—

(a) on conviction on indictment, to imprisonment for life or to a term of imprisonment not less than 10 years;

(b) on summary conviction, to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 12 months or a fine not exceeding level 5 on the standard scale, or to both.

The Government intend to include a power to prescribe exceptions to the right to challenge, in order to protect public bodies from frivolous claims. I will look again at the exceptions, and I am sure we will be looking at them again in Committee.

However, I want to reassure noble Lords that the Bill does not contain an absolute right to challenge a decision. There is no such right in the Human Rights Act 1998, for example. The decision of a public body can only be challenged if the decision is incompatible with the ECHR. That is the test.

The Bill will introduce a positive obligation on public authorities to act compatibly with the ECHR, but it will not prevent public authorities from making incompatible decisions. That is an important distinction. The Bill is not intended to be a vehicle for attacking legitimate public policies. The obligation of compatibility does not prevent a public authority from making a decision which is incompatible with the ECHR. The Bill gives the public authority a defence if the incompatible decision was made in good faith. The court will be able to take into account all the circumstances of the case, including the resources available to the public authority and the seriousness of the impact of the incompatibility. The Government are satisfied that this defence is consistent with the purpose of the Bill.

I assure the noble Lord, Lord Hunt, that, as my right honourable friend the Home Secretary has said, the Government are committed to full implementation of the ECHR, and we have made clear our intention to ensure that the Bill creates the right balance between the rights of the individual and the legitimate needs of public authorities.

There is a bigger issue that the Committee, and indeed the whole House, has to grapple with: how do we use the internet to keep children safe in a world in which they can be exposed to appalling images of abuse and exploitation, whether it is live or recorded?

The answer is complex, but I will try to be clear about some of the issues.

First, we need to do more to work with parents and carers to build their confidence in how to handle the internet. We must do more to educate them about how to ensure that their children are safe from these images.

Secondly, we need to use technology to ensure that children are not exposed to these images. The Home Office is doing more on this, and I commend the work of its child exploitation and online protection centre.

Thirdly, we need to continue to work with internet providers to ensure that they take these images down as fast as possible when they are reported to them. I do not underestimate the complexity of that task. It is a huge challenge and one that requires the full co-operation of the internet providers.

Fourthly, we need to work with the police and other law enforcement agencies to make sure that these images are removed and that the perpetrators are prosecuted. It is right that we are taking a tough line with those who abuse children, and we should continue to do so.

Finally, we need to work with other countries to tackle the problem at source. The internet knows no boundaries, and if there is a paedophile ring in a country such as India, we need to do all we can to work with that country to take action against such activity.

I will continue to work to make sure that we do all we can to keep children safe from this appalling abuse, whether live or recorded.

On the 10th anniversary of the Ukrainian Revolution of Dignity, we must remember that our commitment to Ukraine’s sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity and European perspective is not just a commitment to Ukraine but to the entire region.

This is why, while we should not allow the war in Ukraine to divide us, we must also be realistic. The West must not shy away from taking the necessary steps to ensure we are all safe from Russian aggression.

We must strengthen the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation. We must help Ukraine defend itself.

We must support Ukraine’s integration into the European Union and NATO.

And we must continue to show solidarity with Ukraine, as the UK has done with its military support, its humanitarian aid and the sanctions on Russia.

The war in Ukraine is not just an assault on a sovereign European nation. It is an assault on the European values that define who we are.

Our security is not something to be bought or traded.

It is not something to be taken away or bartered.

It is ours. It is yours. And it will be ours.

Ukraine will be free.

Ukraine will win.

And Ukraine will be in the European Union.

That is not a point of order for me. It is for the Cabinet Secretary.

As I am sure the whole House will agree, violence against women and girls is a despicable crime, which is why it is so important that we take a stand and do everything we can to prevent it.

They have also committed an extra £50 million to tackle violence against women and girls.

In 2014, the Government announced a landmark action plan, the strategy for ending violence against women and girls. This plan has a three-pronged approach, which will be familiar to many Members. Thirdly, it will punish perpetrators, so that they can no longer get away with their crimes.

The strategy also includes a focus on violence against women and girls in the private sphere, which includes domestic abuse and sexual violence, as well as violence in the public sphere, which includes street harassment and sexual harassment.

Let me just put a couple of things in perspective here. In 2016, when the Iran nuclear deal was struck, Iran had some 19,000 centrifuges, of which 1,000 were operating. Now it has 16,000 centrifuges, of which 6,000 are operating. In the same period, the regime has doubled its stock of enriched uranium and built 1,000 more advanced centrifuges. The regime has also installed advanced centrifuges at a secret facility in Natanz and at Fordow, a fortified facility buried inside a mountain. The regime has refused to cooperate with the UN nuclear watchdog, the IAEA, or to allow inspectors to access military sites, as required by the deal. The regime has threatened to enrich uranium to 20%—the level needed for a nuclear bomb. It has also threatened to build up its stock of heavy water, another key ingredient for a bomb, to 130 tonnes—20 times the limit set in the deal.

Let us be clear about what is happening here. Iran is flagrantly breaching the nuclear deal and making a mockery of the international community. research project to identify the main barriers to the delivery of social housing and to identify potential solutions to address these barriers. The research involved a review of international experience and interviews with a range of stakeholders.

The report, Social housing delivery: international experience and emerging Irish issues, was published in November 2017. It found that the barriers to social housing delivery in Ireland are related to the availability and cost of land, and the complexity of the planning process. Other barriers include the limited scope of the Part V planning requirements and the current structure of social housing, which is based on a system of public housing providers.

The report made a number of recommendations, including:

- The need to address land availability and cost, including through a review of the planning process;
- A review of Part V of the Planning and Development Act to ensure that the full scope of the provision is used;
- A review of the structure of social housing to facilitate the delivery of more social housing;
- The need for increased investment in social housing; and
- The need for a new national strategy for social housing.

The Government, in the context of the Rebuilding Ireland Action Plan for Housing and Homelessness, is currently developing a new social housing strategy, which will include a new strategic approach to addressing social housing issues. The strategy will aim to:

- Make best use of existing resources and maximise the impact of investment;
- Support the implementation of the Rebuilding Ireland Action Plan for Housing and Homelessness; and
- Promote the delivery of social housing.

The new strategy will be supported by the publication of a national social housing delivery plan. The Department of Housing, Planning and Local Government is also examining how planning and development legislation, including Part V, could be amended to facilitate social housing delivery, and is examining proposals for a new delivery mechanism.

What does the act do?

The Multiculturalism Act recognizes the cultural and ethnic diversity of Canada and Canada's linguistic duality. It commits the federal government to:

- Take measures to preserve and enhance the multicultural heritage of Canadians.
- Take measures to preserve and enhance the multilingual and multicultural heritage of Canada.

The federal government may fund projects, programs and activities that preserve and enhance the multicultural heritage of Canadians and take measures to preserve and enhance the multilingual and multicultural heritage of Canada.

Which projects are eligible for funding?

Eligible projects:

- Promote understanding and respect between ethnocultural communities.
- Promote the full participation of members of ethnocultural communities in the economic, social and cultural life of Canada.
- Support the integration of members of ethnocultural communities into Canadian society.

Ineligible projects:

- Do not respect the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
- Do not respect human rights.
- Support conversion to one or another religion or religious belief.
- Advocate hatred or intolerance.
- Are contrary to public policy.

For more information about the Multiculturalism Act, visit www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/services/multiculturalism-act.html

Scotland’s legal position is unchanged as a result of the UK leaving the EU.

There is no constitutional or legal requirement for the Scottish Parliament to grant legislative consent to the UK Government on any legislation that may affect Scotland as a result of the UK leaving the EU.

If the Scottish Parliament were to express a view on the legislation, it is for the UK Government to decide how it should respond.

This was made clear in our briefing to the UK Government in advance of the introduction of the Withdrawal Bill and is reflected in the agreement reached between the Scottish and UK Governments on the Withdrawal Bill.

In addition to the UK Government’s undertaking to work to secure a legislative consent motion, the agreement also set out that the UK Government would keep under review any possible further powers for the Scottish Parliament.

Distracted driving is also a significant cause of injury crashes, with the highest rates of distracted driving crashes occurring among drivers aged 20-29. It is estimated that about 65% of all distracted driving crashes involve drivers who are 20-29 years old.

### What is Distracted Driving?

The term “distracted driving” refers to any activity that diverts a person’s attention away from the primary task of driving. Any non-driving activity you engage in while operating a motor vehicle is distracted driving.

Examples of distracted driving include the following:

- Talking or texting on a cell phone
- Using a cell phone to check for email or send text messages
- Using a cell phone to take a photo or video
- Using a cell phone to access the Internet
- Talking to other passengers in the vehicle
- Grooming
- Reading (including maps)
- Using a navigation system
- Eating or drinking
- Adjusting a radio, CD player, or MP3 player
- Watching a video
- Smoking

### Distracted Driving is Dangerous

Distracted driving significantly increases the risk of being involved in a car accident. You are 23 times more likely to crash while texting and driving than you are while driving without distractions.

### Older Persons Services

Ireland is now the oldest country in the EU, with almost 900,000 people aged over 65. The proportion of older people in the population is increasing. There will be approximately 1.35 million people aged over 65 by 2021, 1.55 million by 2026 and 1.69 million by 2031.

Ireland’s ageing population is a major challenge for all sectors of society, but a particular challenge for health and social care services. While population ageing is generally regarded as a positive development, it will have implications for the delivery of health and social care services and for the workforce that delivers these services.

The Irish Health Service Executive National Older Person Services Programme (OPSP) has a national goal of providing person-centred, integrated, high quality health and social care services that enable older people to remain independent and engaged in their communities.

The OPSP is a five-year programme, which commenced in 2018 and is being implemented by the HSE. The programme has a budget of €100 million in 2020.

A new book has just come out, edited by David Dutton and Richard Toye, about the extent to which the British people in the 1930s were prepared to fight for their country in a war against Germany. The book is called Britain and the Second World War: Public Attitudes and Opinions and is published by Palgrave.

The book is of particular interest to me because one of the chapters is by my father, Professor Tony Kushner. His chapter looks at the attitudes of Jewish people in Britain to the possibility of war.

I’ve always been curious about the way in which my father, born in 1940, has been shaped by the legacy of the Second World War. My father is the son of Jewish refugees from Germany, and his parents arrived in Britain in the early 1930s.

Their flight from Germany was not so much a flight from Nazism, which was still seen at that time by many people as a localised German problem, but rather a flight from persecution by the German authorities, which had been going on since the late 1920s. As Professor Kushner makes clear in his chapter in the new book, there were many Jews in Germany who did not take the threat to their lives and their children’s lives seriously, and many people in the Jewish community who were actively opposed to their emigration from Germany.

For those who did emigrate, there was no certainty that they would be welcomed, and there were many places in the world where Jews were still being persecuted and often murdered.

The UK, which had the most liberal immigration policy in the world in the 1930s, provided a haven for many Jews, but it was by no means the only one. Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and a few other places also welcomed Jewish refugees

I would like to argue that the concept of sustainability should be applied to all types of policy decisions. Consider for example a policy that provides subsidies for the purchase of hybrid cars. Such a policy will have an impact on the number of people who purchase hybrid cars. It may also have a knock-on effect on the number of other cars that will be purchased by people who would otherwise have purchased hybrids. That is, such a policy may increase the number of cars on the road.

A subsidy for the purchase of hybrid cars is not necessarily unsustainable. If the increase in cars on the road is not excessive and there is a net reduction in the emission of greenhouse gases, then the subsidy may be sustainable. On the other hand, the policy may be unsustainable if the increase in cars is excessive and the policy does not lead to a net reduction in the emission of greenhouse gases. The important thing is to consider the impact of the policy on future generations and how such a policy should be evaluated.

Another example of a policy that may be unsustainable is a policy of free education. Such a policy may be sustainable if there is no significant increase in the number of students who enroll in universities. In addition, the policy should not have a negative impact on the quality of education. However, the policy may be unsustainable if the policy increases the number of students and reduces the quality of education.

A policy may be sustainable if the impact on future generations is taken into account. This concept can be applied to a wide range of policies and is particularly important in the area of environmental policy.

It is the solemn duty of our government to remember the victims of the Holocaust and to honour their sacrifice. It is the duty of our society to ensure that lessons are learned from history and to combat hatred and persecution.

We are all united in our revulsion at the evil of the Holocaust. We remember the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust and the millions of other victims of Nazi persecution, including Roma, the disabled, and LGBT+ people.

We stand shoulder to shoulder with survivors and their families and pay tribute to their strength, courage and resilience.

As we mark Holocaust Memorial Day 2023, we remember the victims of the Holocaust, the Roma genocide and other Nazi persecutions. We reaffirm our commitment to remembering the past, learning from it and uniting against hatred, prejudice and bigotry.

Together, we say never again.

This new approach to HTA was introduced in 2005. The Department of Health and Children (DoHC) published its New Drugs Guidelines (NDGs) and a list of medicines for which the NDGs would be applied. In addition to the NDGs, the HSE has also been applying a second HTA approach to new medicines: the Pricing and Reimbursement Guidelines (PRGs). The NDGs are an HTA approach, and as such, they focus on the clinical value of a new medicine (and how this compares with other treatment options) and its cost-effectiveness. The PRGs are a health technology assessment approach, and as such, they focus on the cost of a medicine in comparison to its cost-effectiveness.

The Consumer Protection (Distance Selling) Regulations 2000 (Regulations) were introduced in order to protect consumers in relation to the sale of goods and services. These Regulations provide that consumers are able to cancel contracts entered into at a distance within seven working days, without giving any reason. In order to avail of this right, consumers must give notice to the trader that they wish to cancel the contract within the seven-day period. If the consumer does not do this, they will not be able to cancel the contract. The Regulations do not apply to contracts which are negotiated at an auction.

There are certain exceptions to this right to cancel. The most relevant of these exceptions is the exception in relation to contracts for the supply of goods, services or digital content which are personalised to the consumer’s specifications. This exception means that if a consumer has requested that the product be personalised to their specification, they will not be able to cancel the contract. The Regulations also provide that, where a contract is concluded via a form of distance communication that was initiated by the consumer, the consumer will not be able to cancel the contract.

In CETA, there is a provision that is very similar to the Trans-Pacific Partnership, with some language changes. I think that the two provisions in the Trans-Pacific Partnership and CETA are very similar and are a good template to be used for the new Canada-United States-Mexico agreement.

There is no one-size-fits-all solution to this problem. Lithium-ion battery thermal runaway is a complex chemical reaction that has not yet been fully understood. It is necessary to do research on each type of lithium-ion battery, as well as on each product that contains one of these batteries, to discover what is causing the thermal runaway. In addition, manufacturers and safety officials need to understand the factors that cause thermal runaway and how to prevent it.

The US has a great deal of expertise and experience in dealing with lithium-ion batteries. However, because these batteries are in so many different types of products, it is difficult to regulate the manufacturers or product designers. The US does not have the authority to regulate batteries in products that are not considered consumer goods. For instance, there are no federal regulations for the design of airplane batteries or for the design of the battery compartment in a mobile phone.

The Department of Transportation, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) do have authority over lithium-ion batteries in consumer goods. However, they are not the primary authority on lithium-ion battery safety. The responsibility for ensuring that a lithium-ion battery is safe lies with the product manufacturer or designer.

The Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) is the federal agency that investigates battery fires, and it can order a recall if the batteries are found to be dangerous. The FAA also has the authority to regulate airplane batteries. The FCC has the authority to investigate lithium-ion batteries in mobile phones and to order recalls. However, the FCC does not have the authority to order the recall of a mobile phone.

Ireland is not the first European country to ban fur farming. Denmark banned mink farming in 1989, Sweden did the same in 1998 and Norway in 2009. Ireland should be proud to be taking this step to ban fur farming. It’s a positive step to align Ireland’s animal welfare legislation with our values as a society.

Fur farming is cruel and inhumane, it is not conducive to good animal welfare and it is not sustainable.

There is a lot of public support for the ban. The majority of people in Ireland are against fur farming and according to a survey in the UK in 2017, 85% of the public are opposed to fur farming.

Fur farming is unsustainable. The animals kept for fur are usually killed before they reach adulthood. A typical mink has a life expectancy of 5 years, however, farmed mink are killed after 7 months. A mink’s fur only grows in the spring and summer so the animals are killed at a time when they should be at their most healthy and active.

Fur farming is a threat to human health. The mink on fur farms are prone to illnesses. Mink on farms can carry bacteria and viruses like Salmonella, Campylobacter, E.coli and Brucella. The animals are also prone to parasites like mites, lice and ticks. The animals on farms are often sick, stressed and depressed and this makes them vulnerable to disease. Mink can be a source of many diseases that can affect humans and animals.

## Child Maintenance Laws

The Child Maintenance Service (CMS) is the DWP agency responsible for setting the amount of maintenance that is payable and enforcing payment. The CMS only deals with maintenance cases where there is a split of residence between the parents. Where the parents live together, the CMS cannot help.

Maintenance is payable to a parent with care of the child where the other parent has a higher income. The CMS sets a “basic rate” of maintenance based on the payer’s income. If the payer wishes to pay more, they can do so by making a “voluntary top-up”.

Maintenance can be paid either directly to the parent with care by the payer, or indirectly to the CMS and then to the parent with care. If the payer fails to pay the maintenance, the CMS will enforce payment.

## Child Maintenance Enforcement

Where the payer fails to make payment, there are a number of options available to the CMS to enforce payment:

- The CMS can “instruct” a payer’s employer to make deductions from the payer’s salary to cover the amount owed.
- The CMS can apply for an attachment of earnings order through the courts to require the payer’s employer to make deductions.
- The CMS can apply for a charging order to require a payer to pay a lump sum from the proceeds of sale of any property the payer owns.
- The CMS can request the DWP to make deductions from the payer’s benefits to cover the arrears.

The reasons for the backlog are multifaceted. According to the Citizenship and Immigration Canada, 80 percent of the backlog is due to the large number of applicants who have submitted incomplete applications, or have not provided adequate information to immigration officers. It is also due to the increasing number of applicants, the growing complexity of the applications, and a high volume of appeals.

The lengthy waits for approval are not only frustrating, but for many, a source of extreme anxiety. People who have waited two or three years to be approved are now starting to lose hope that their applications will ever be approved.

What is more, the frustration of waiting for approval is only one of many difficulties faced by people who have been waiting for permanent residency. Many have difficulty getting their applications processed due to the many requirements that need to be met. Other applicants have been rejected due to errors in the applications, or for not submitting the required supporting documentation.

The wait is further compounded by the fact that the system is not designed to accommodate the high volume of applications. The backlog of applications and appeals are a problem that needs to be addressed, but for now, the only way to get the process moving forward is to file a formal appeal with the IRCC. If you have been denied approval, you should seek the advice of a qualified immigration lawyer.

The Social Welfare Act 2011 introduced a new income threshold of €5,000 for the purposes of the calculation of means for certain benefits. This new threshold has been applied since January 2011.

The Bill amends the Act to remove the requirement to have been in receipt of means tested social welfare payments for at least 26 weeks in the 60 weeks prior to a means test being carried out.

Education and Training Boards

The Bill amends the Education and Training Boards Act 2013 to provide for the dissolution of the further and higher education bodies in accordance with section 18 of the Education Act 1998.

Under section 60 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, police have the power to stop and search in specified areas or at specified events. The purpose of the Bill is to allow police to stop and search in designated areas without having to specify that area beforehand. If Parliament Square were designated as an area for suspicionless stop and search, police would not be able to search anyone. The police officer would have to have a reasonable suspicion of criminal activity before being able to stop and search. In the case of a Member of Parliament or a member of staff of the House, the police officer would need to have a reasonable suspicion that they were committing a crime before being able to stop and search them.

### Natural gas is a cleaner, more efficient fuel for heating and electricity generation.

#### What is Natural Gas?

Natural gas is a natural resource that is composed primarily of methane, with other gases including ethane, propane, butane, pentane, and heptane, among others. It is found in the Earth’s crust and is located in reservoirs. Natural gas is extracted and distributed through a series of pipelines.

#### What is LNG?

Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) is natural gas that has been liquefied. Natural gas is converted to a liquid by cooling it to -162 degrees Celsius. LNG can be stored in tanks and shipped in specially built LNG tankers.

#### What is NGV?

Natural Gas Vehicle (NGV) is a vehicle that operates on compressed natural gas (CNG) or liquefied natural gas (LNG). NGVs can be equipped with dual-fuel engines to operate on both natural gas and gasoline or diesel.

#### What is NGP?

Natural Gas Power (NGP) is the process of generating electricity by burning natural gas in a power plant.

## What is the definition of a close contact?

The definition of a close contact is someone who has been within 1 meter for more than 15 minutes. This includes in school or in the classroom, for example, but not necessarily at home. If a child is in the same classroom as someone who has tested positive, they are not considered to be a close contact and so do not need to be sent home.

The government’s first offer, a customs partnership with the EU, was dead on arrival. It was not even workable. The Treasury told the Prime Minister that it would be very expensive, if not impossible to implement. There were also questions about its legality, and the risk that it would tie our hands for future trade agreements with the rest of the world.

The Prime Minister’s second offer, the Chequers agreement, was an improvement, but it still had a number of problems. It was not a free trade agreement, and it would not have taken us out of the EU’s customs union and single market. It would have given the EU the power to set our trade rules and regulations, and it would have tied us to EU institutions and policies.

The Prime Minister’s third offer, the backstop proposal, is an even worse deal. It would have bound the UK into a customs union with the EU for an indefinite period of time, with no guarantee that we would get out of it in the end. It would have created a customs border in the Irish sea, undermining the integrity of the United Kingdom, and it would have removed our ability to strike free trade agreements with the rest of the world, including the United States and Australia.

The Prime Minister has been unable to get her deals through Parliament because they have been bad deals. The Covid-19 pandemic has resulted in an unprecedented impact on transport, both in terms of its operation and its finances. In terms of operation, there have been severe reductions in passenger numbers, with the lowest point in public transport being a 95% reduction in demand on our rail network on 29 March 2020. There have been severe impacts on the finances of transport operators and, indeed, transport users. ## Examinations in the coming year

In light of the ongoing public health restrictions, including the continued closure of schools to all but small groups of students, the Department of Education will work with the State Examinations Commission to provide for examinations in the coming academic year.

The main issue facing the examination system is the need to ensure that the grades that students are awarded are a fair reflection of the work they have done throughout the year. Given the considerable disruption to the learning of students, the State Examinations Commission will develop a fair process to award grades to students. The grades awarded will be based on the performance of students in school assessments, taking into account the considerable disruption to the learning of students, and on the evidence available to teachers in the school. The process will also include a review of school work by the State Examinations Commission in order to ensure that the grades awarded are fair and accurate.

The Government is committed to working closely with the education partners to support the State Examinations Commission in developing a process that is fair and reasonable for students.

The State Examinations Commission will publish a further statement to provide further details on the examinations process in the coming academic year.

The 2017 general election provided a mandate for the Government to pursue a new industrial strategy for the United Kingdom. We believe that a well-functioning economy can only be built on a foundation of strong communities. The UK Government believe that there is more that needs to be done to empower those communities, and we have set out our agenda for social reform in the form of a white paper, which we plan to publish before the end of the year.

The Government’s industrial strategy will be a radical departure from the past. It will not be a prescriptive centrally driven programme but will be based on co-designing and co-delivering policies with business, local government and civil society. It will build on the UK’s strengths, including world-class universities, highly skilled work force and financial sector, while also recognising that not all communities have benefited equally from economic success in recent years.

The Government recognise that inequality of opportunity is one of the most pressing challenges facing our country. We are determined to tackle inequality, particularly inequality that is driven by where people live. We recognise that communities and local areas across the country have very different needs and that some areas have experienced significant and persistent disadvantage.

##### CIL

How is the Government proposing to address the issue of land banking?

The Government has introduced a new Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) on development in England. The aim of the levy is to provide a financial contribution towards the infrastructure required to support new development. CIL is a charge on the development rather than on the land owner. This charge is then used to help pay for infrastructure, including affordable housing, to support new development.

The levy will apply to new build in England, including conversions of houses or offices into housing, and will be set by local authorities. It will only apply to developments which are larger than a certain size. The Government estimates that CIL will generate £200 million per annum for infrastructure. This is in addition to the New Homes Bonus, which is also being introduced.

The Government has not yet published details of the system for Northern Ireland.

##### Planning for Growth

The Government has also published a consultation on Planning for Growth, which deals with the relationship between CIL, the New Homes Bonus, and the Community Right to Build.

The Government is proposing to introduce a right to build for local communities. This would allow community groups to develop small sites of land for housing without the need for planning permission. Under this system, local communities could apply to develop a site, and if the land owner does not object, then the planning permission is automatically granted.

In 2001, the Irish Government introduced legislation legalising abortion in the case of risk to the life of the mother, including risk of suicide.

The Protection of Life During Pregnancy Act 2013 (PLDPA) allows for abortion in the case of threat to life – including risk of suicide. The Act also allows for abortion in the case of a fatal foetal abnormality. The Act requires a second opinion from another doctor and a High Court judge must give permission for an abortion. The Act also allows for a third party to bring proceedings to secure an abortion if the woman is deemed incapable of making a decision.

There is no provision in the Act for an abortion in the case of rape or incest.

The PLDPA is a deeply flawed Act, which undermines the sanctity of life and the right to life of the unborn child, and puts doctors, nurses and midwives in an impossible situation of having to choose between their conscience and their job.

This legislation allows for a third party to bring proceedings to secure an abortion on behalf of a woman who is deemed incapable of making a decision.

The PLDPA is undermining the right to freedom of conscience and is violating the conscience rights of doctors, nurses and midwives. In the case of Marie v. An Bord Uchtála,  the Supreme Court held that the PLDPA violates the constitutional right to freedom of conscience.

Doctors, nurses and midwives are calling for the repeal of the PLDPA and for conscience rights to be protected by law.

## Abortion in Ireland

A woman can seek a legal abortion in Ireland for reasons of risk to her life if she can secure a certificate from two medical consultants and an order from a High Court judge.

The State is investing €500 million in the national broadband plan. A further €116 million is being provided by the European Regional Development Fund.

This funding is providing for fibre to the home broadband for all households in rural Ireland that do not have access to broadband.

This plan is being delivered by a consortium of four companies: Granahan McCourt, SSE Airtricity, Vodafone and SIRO.

The national broadband plan is a major State infrastructure investment. The project is a public private partnership and the State is making a substantial investment.

The national broadband plan is in the final stages of procurement and there are ongoing contract negotiations.

I am aware that it is taking too long to deliver fibre broadband to rural Ireland. The Government is very conscious of this and Minister Cannon and I have been engaging with the Department to ensure that all resources are being used to deliver the project.

The national broadband plan is a major infrastructure project which will deliver a new technology to rural Ireland. This is being done in a very short period of time. The first phase of the project is being delivered on time, and work is ongoing with the consortium to deliver the second phase as soon as possible.

In the meantime, the Department is continuing to provide a subsidy to providers to deliver broadband to the unserved and underserved.

This is another delay tactic, as Mr. Lametti has been invited to testify on April 25, so his testimony will occur before the Prime Minister’s. The Prime Minister has also stated he would only testify on the condition he would have the right to make a “closing statement” at the end of the testimony of all the witnesses. This is another delay tactic, as it will ensure he would be the last to testify, and it will ensure the committee does not have any follow-up questions for him.

Finally, the Prime Minister has stated he would testify only if his testimony would be released “as soon as possible” after his testimony. The purpose of the consultation was to gather information and views from the general public, businesses and other stakeholders on how best to tackle food waste in Ireland. The roadmap will serve as a key document for Government policy-makers and stakeholders to reduce food waste.

A food waste prevention roadmap is a document that provides a framework for how to tackle food waste and the development of a strategy in a particular country. A roadmap sets out the current status of food waste in a country, outlines the existing policy and legislative context and defines a clear vision for the future, with measurable targets. It also outlines the necessary actions, stakeholders and resources needed to achieve the roadmap’s objectives.

The consultation document was published for a 12-week period. The response received was very positive with 271 responses received. The responses came from a wide range of stakeholders including businesses, local authorities, NGOs, waste management companies and individuals. The results of the consultation are now being analysed and a final national food waste prevention roadmap is due to be published later this year.

My Department will continue to work with all stakeholders to achieve the vision of a society where food is never wasted.

The National Food Waste Prevention Roadmap Consultation Document can be found on my Department’s website at: https://www.agriculture.gov.ie/foodwastemap/foodwastemap.pdf

The Bill does not impose new restrictions or conditions on the devolved Administrations. It does not introduce any new taxes. Let me take a step back. The UK is a union of nations. The devolution settlements set out how powers are distributed between the UK and the devolved Administrations and what conditions must be met if a power is transferred from the UK to the devolved Administrations. The devolution settlements are not statutory. They are constitutional arrangements that are made between the four nations of the UK. The devolution settlements set out the distribution of powers between the UK and the devolved Administrations and the conditions for any future transfer of powers from the UK.

The powers to make laws for a devolved nation are reserved to the UK Parliament by the devolution settlements, but it is not possible to say exactly which powers are reserved to the UK Parliament or which are devolved to the devolved Administrations. The Budget this year will see a £12 billion deficit in 2014-15. We have an annual deficit of £1.5 billion and in the last few years we have seen the highest levels of borrowing since World War II. The Chancellor has made it clear that the Government needs to get its finances in order. We do not have unlimited resources. The country has been living beyond its means for far too long and we have to reduce this deficit. This is the only way to guarantee that we do not pass on more debts to our children and grandchildren.

As a country, we have been living in a fantasy world. We have lived beyond our means, we have spent more than we have earned and we have borrowed far too much money. We can no longer afford to live like this. We have to make some tough decisions.

## What Single Mothers Face

Single mothers face many challenges. They are often seen as less capable of raising their children than two-parent families. This is not true. Single mothers are just as capable of raising children as two-parent families.

However, single mothers often face financial hardship. They may be on a fixed income, and it can be challenging to make ends meet. They may not have enough money to provide for their children’s needs.

Single mothers may also be struggling to find childcare. It can be challenging to find affordable, quality childcare, and it can be even more difficult for single mothers. They may have to work long hours to make ends meet, leaving them with little time to find quality childcare.

Another challenge that single mothers face is that they may be stigmatized. They may be seen as less capable of raising their children than two-parent families. This is not true. Single mothers are just as capable of raising children as two-parent families. However, they may be judged for their decision to raise their children alone.

## How To Help Single Mothers

If you know a single mother, there are many ways you can help. You can offer to watch her children so she can take a break, or you can help with errands or other tasks.

Bill Teron graduated from the University of Manitoba with a degree in civil engineering and it was this degree that would eventually lead him to Ottawa. ## Are hospices only for people with cancer?

Hospice care is not only for people with cancer. Many other conditions qualify for hospice care. While cancer is one of the most common reasons for receiving hospice care, hospice services are available to people with all kinds of terminal illnesses.

## Do hospice nurses make a difference?

The Nursing Home Quality Initiative found that hospice care improved the quality of care for hospice patients in nursing homes. Specifically, hospice care was associated with lower rates of medication errors, hospitalizations, falls, and pressure ulcers, and higher rates of satisfaction with care.

## Do hospice patients get massages?

Many hospice patients request massage to reduce pain, relieve tension and stress, and increase feelings of comfort. Massage can be a very effective addition to a hospice care plan, and the benefits can last even after the session ends.

## What is the main role of the hospice nurse?

Hospice nurses provide compassionate care to patients and their families. They support families through the process of end-of-life care. Hospice nurses coordinate patient care plans. They also provide education to families and patients, and assist with physical care needs.

When do patients qualify for hospice care? When determining eligibility for hospice, a doctor must certify that you’re terminally ill, with a life expectancy of six months or less if the disease runs its expected course.

### Omicron is Not an Alarming Variant

### Omicron Has Spread Rapidly

The State cannot impose a view on any citizen in respect of any particular moral issue and it cannot interfere with a person's fundamental right to freedom of conscience or expression. It is important to strike the right balance between protecting a doctor's right to conscience and ensuring that patients and the public are protected. The State has a duty to protect patients, both from the actions of doctors and from doctors' inaction. It also has a duty to protect the public from harm or inconvenience.

If a doctor refuses to prescribe contraception or abortion pills to a patient, there is a duty on the State to ensure that there is an alternative source of contraception and abortion pills. The Bill is based on the principles of conscience and conscience protection. It is consistent with the provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights in that it provides for a right of conscientious objection and it provides that a doctor who exercises his or her right of conscientious objection may not be penalised. It is not a complete opt-out for a doctor and a doctor cannot refuse to provide care to a person in an emergency. There are other exceptions, and I will deal with them in a moment. There are also requirements in the Bill for doctors to ensure that other doctors are available to provide the service in question, if the doctor objects to it, and for doctors to inform the patient in good time if they object to the treatment being prescribed.

The Bill is not an attempt by the Government to force doctors to do something which offends their moral or religious beliefs. The Bill simply requires that doctors provide a service to which they are objecting but which is lawful in this State and for which there is a demand in the community. The main reason for the flood was the lack of capacity at the Cork weir on the Lee River. The flood barriers were not built high enough to cope with the volume of water coming down the Lee. The weir was built to stop the river rising to a height of 11.8m. That is 1.8m above its level before the floods.

This would have prevented the water from flowing under the road, causing the water to rise up the river in the valley.

The Government is talking about lowering the river again to reduce the risk of flooding. I would like to see a consultation between all the interested parties including the ESB, Cork County Council, the National Roads Authority, Cork City Council and the Office of Public Works to see how the weir can be raised and the capacity increased to prevent future floods.

What we need to do is to get the water out of the valley and down to Cork harbour as fast as possible. The weir should be raised to a level which will prevent the river flooding the road again.

I agree that the road is important. However, so is the safety of our emergency services, the residents of the villages and the people who work in the valley.

If we don't prevent flooding again, people will die the next time.

committed to ensuring our veterans are provided with the tools and resources they need to successfully transition into a new life in the civilian economy.

Women in the military face a particular set of challenges due to the historical under-representation of women in the Canadian Armed Forces. For instance, 99 per cent of women veterans in Canada have children compared with 91 per cent of men veterans. In addition, female veterans are more likely to report having a physical disability due to their service, and less likely to have completed a post-secondary education compared with their male counterparts.

In 2017, our government made it a priority to help women transition back into the civilian economy. Through our support for the Women in the Military Transition Table, women veterans can access the information, programs and services they need, including those provided by Veterans Affairs Canada and Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC), to succeed in their new lives.

Our government also recently announced an investment of $17.6 million in Budget 2019 to support the Veteran Family Well-Being Fund. This initiative will work with partners to address the needs of families as veterans transition out of the military.

Budget 2019 also announced a new pilot project to support women in the Canadian Armed Forces as they transition into the civilian workforce. The Veteran Women in Technology program will provide eligible women with access to supports to address the unique barriers they face as they look for work, including training, education and job placement. The program will help women in the Canadian Armed Forces develop the skills they need to access the high-demand technology sector in Canada.

Our government is committed to supporting all of our veterans. As a proud military family, we are working to ensure that all women veterans receive the resources they need to help them transition back into the civilian workforce.

## Regional Waste Management Offices

There are three regional waste management offices in Ireland. These are:

East Regional Waste Management Office, which covers Dublin, Kildare, Louth, Meath, Wicklow, Wexford and Carlow.

South Regional Waste Management Office, which covers Cork, Kerry, Waterford and Limerick.

West Regional Waste Management Office, which covers Clare, Galway, Leitrim, Longford, Mayo, Roscommon, Sligo and Donegal.

These offices provide a range of waste management planning and support services for local authorities in their respective regions.

### History

The area was first developed for docking in the early 18th century, under the name of Upper Hope, and became known as the Upper Dock in 1871. From 1894 it became known as the Strood Dock, and in 1932 the name was changed to Strood Docks.

### Facilities

Facilities at the docks include:

- 130 acres of open storage space
- 25 acres of covered storage
- A 125 tonne gantry crane with a reach of 21 metres
- Berthing facilities for vessels up to 100 metres in length

### Facts about the Strood Docks

The Strood Docks have an interesting history, including the following facts:

- They were the first docks to be built in Kent
- They were built by Henry Fludyer, a local merchant
- They were designed by Thomas Wright
- They were originally used for coal, which was brought to the dock on barges from Newcastle-upon-Tyne
- They were acquired by the Port of London Authority in 1911

But in this edition of the ASIO review, our new director-general Duncan Lewis challenges this view. He observes: “I disagree. There is nothing new about this environment. The world remains a dangerous place, and it always has been.”

The world today is as dangerous as it has ever been and it always has been. As the world has changed, so have the threats. They now include state and non-state actors, conventional and unconventional threats, and kinetic and non-kinetic threats.

And these threats have the potential to become hybrid threats, as illustrated by Russia’s annexation of Crimea. The threat is not just the acquisition of Crimea but the use of cyber, disinformation and information warfare. The use of this combination of threats will be more common in the future.

State-based threats are also not a new phenomenon, and there will always be rogue states that are seeking to undermine the rules-based order. In the 1960s, the Soviet Union was a rogue state. Today it is Russia and China.

As a result, ASIO will continue to play an important role in keeping Australia safe, as we have since 1949.

The agency’s role is not just to identify threats but to work with other government agencies and the private sector to prevent them from becoming a reality.

To illustrate this point, the review provides a number of examples of where ASIO has prevented the country from being subject to a terrorist attack. It also details how ASIO has worked with other agencies and the private sector to minimise the impact of the cyber threat.

At the same time, the world is changing. The ASIO review outlines how the agency has changed over the past decade—in particular since 9/11—to keep up with the times.

The Minister’s final reason given for not supporting the amendments was that the Act already provides for a broad discretion for the Minister to determine the amount of compensation payable to a person in respect of an unlawful search and seizure.

The Act does provide for the Minister to determine the amount of compensation payable in certain circumstances. However, the problem with this provision is that it is inconsistent with the provisions of the Bill of Rights, specifically the right to a fair hearing and the right to just administrative action.

The right to a fair hearing guarantees the right to a hearing before a court of law, while the right to just administrative action guarantees the right to have a decision reviewed by an impartial court of law.

When the State undertakes an unlawful search and seizure, it does so unilaterally. There is no legal requirement for it to go to a court of law or even to notify the owner that it has undertaken a search or seized property. The person’s only remedy is to apply to the Minister for compensation. As the person is not informed that his property has been searched or seized, or what has been taken, he or she will only know after the fact.

Another issue that has been raised in the context of the MH17 shoot-down, and also in relation to other issues such as the missing Malaysian airliner, MH370, is the issue of the capacity of the ATSB.

The ATSB has a role in relation to Australian aircraft. But, if we are to accept that there is an international responsibility in relation to international air space, then it would seem to be the case that an appropriate body would need to be established and funded with the resources and authority to conduct a proper investigation in such circumstances.

I would not say that this is the ATSB’s fault, because I do not believe that the ATSB has the resources to undertake that sort of work, as it is already overworked with the sort of work it does. But the point I am making is that, if we are to be a part of the international community, then we have to contribute to the international investigation of such incidents. That means that there would have to be a body, and it would have to be funded appropriately, to be able to undertake that work.

That means it would have to be able to deal with the international intelligence agencies that are operating, not only in our own country, but in the countries that are directly involved, in terms of the shooting-down of the MH17 aircraft. It would have to deal with intelligence agencies such as the United States intelligence agencies, the Russian intelligence agencies, the Chinese intelligence agencies, the Malaysian intelligence agencies, the Indonesian intelligence agencies, and the Ukrainian intelligence agencies.

Therefore, it is not just a matter of having the capability to investigate what happened. It is a matter of having the capability to deal with all the other issues that are involved.

The proposed offence includes an element of "departure or attempted departure from the State". In the case of Irish nationals, this would be a departure from the State to a foreign country. In the case of non-Irish nationals, this would be a departure from Ireland, or an attempt to depart from Ireland, to a foreign country.

I ask the Deputy to withdraw amendment No. 73 because it would seek to amend the proposed offence to delete the word "departure". The reference to "departure" in the offence is important in light of the proposed exemptions for humanitarian assistance.

The exemption would apply to a departure from the State by a person to provide humanitarian assistance in a foreign country, or to travel as part of a team of persons providing humanitarian assistance in a foreign country. In other words, the exemption would apply to a person who departs from the State to provide humanitarian assistance in a foreign country and to a person who departs from the State to join a team of persons providing humanitarian assistance in a foreign country. However, the exemption would not apply to a person who departs from the State to provide humanitarian assistance in the State.

The humanitarian assistance exemption would not apply to persons who are not Irish citizens. The proposed offence would only apply to Irish citizens who depart from the State to provide humanitarian assistance in a foreign country. That is why the offence refers to a "departure from the State". It is important that there be no ambiguity about whether the exemption would apply to persons who are not Irish citizens. The proposed offence would be aimed at preventing Irish citizens from travelling abroad to provide support to terrorist groups.

Canada has a proud history of being a leader in the fight for nuclear disarmament. Canada was an original signatory to the nuclear non-proliferation treaty (NPT) in 1970, and the Canadian government under Lester B. Pearson was instrumental in its drafting.

The nuclear ban treaty (NBT), also known as the treaty on the prohibition of nuclear weapons, was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 2017, and opened for signature in September 2017. Canada was one of 118 nations that voted in favour of the treaty, but Canada has not signed the treaty.

The protest is in order to get the attention of Topshop's parent company, Arcadia, and to highlight the problem that many Irish workers face.

In 2009, when Arcadia decided to close their 76 stores in Ireland, they were legally obliged to pay workers a redundancy package based on two weeks pay for each year of service.

Workers were expecting to receive a redundancy payment of around €300, but instead they received a letter from Arcadia stating that they were not entitled to any redundancy pay, because of a loophole in Irish law.

In 2009, the Irish Employment Rights Act was amended in order to encourage foreign companies to continue to operate in Ireland despite the recession. In the amendment to the legislation, foreign companies were given the power to pay redundancy pay based on the laws of the country where they are registered.

Arcadia decided to take advantage of this and decided to pay the redundancy package based on UK law.

The former Topshop employees are protesting outside the store on Tuesday morning in order to show Topshop customers that Arcadia have cheated their workers. They are urging the public to support them by avoiding the store.

The group are calling on Arcadia to pay workers their redundancy, as they were promised they would. They have already contacted Minister for Jobs Richard Bruton about their issue, but have been met with silence.

Many workers are struggling to survive on the redundancy package they received. Arcadia is currently in the process of opening a new Topshop store in Dublin, but have refused to pay the workers the redundancy that they are owed.

Many of those arriving in Italy this week tell of being held in Libya for up to two years, unable to get any further towards Europe.

Italy’s prime minister Matteo Renzi has called for action, but this is not a problem that can be solved by the Italian government alone.

There needs to be action at the European level. This is an issue of human rights, of solidarity and of international law. European governments need to work together to bring an end to the suffering of people who are trapped in Libya.

If they were given the option of leaving Libya, most would do so tomorrow. They are being held against their will and extorted for money.

It is true that the number of deaths in the Mediterranean has fallen over the last year. But that is not because of the actions of European governments. The number of deaths is down because there has been a huge increase in the number of people being held in Libya.

People who would have otherwise been trying to reach Europe by boat are now being held in Libya for years. These people are not being given an option to leave. The only way they are able to get out of Libya is to pay large sums of money.

There needs to be a concerted effort to provide safe alternatives to the current routes taken by those fleeing war and poverty. A concerted effort to end the suffering of people is needed. The situation is no longer sustainable.

In the context of a rapidly changing work environment, the role of the family is under increasing pressure from the demands of paid employment. In addition, the family is being increasingly subjected to pressures that arise from the changing structure of employment. The reality is that the world of work is changing rapidly and employers are finding it increasingly difficult to manage an ever-growing range of demands on both the employee and the employer.

We are looking at the role of the family in the context of a rapidly changing work environment and of a rapidly changing world of work. We are also looking at the family in the context of a changing family structure.

There is a wide range of family structures in Ireland today. We are living in a world in which the family is under pressure from economic and social developments, and in which the family is becoming a smaller, more nuclear unit. We are looking at the family in the context of a changing world, a changing society and a changing economy. It is clear that in order to maintain the family unit in Ireland we must have a set of policies that will promote the family in a world in which the world of work and the family are in increasing conflict.

Several factors have contributed to the rise in the cost of food. The first is the rising cost of labour. As the cost of living has increased, the cost of labour has also increased. The cost of labour is a major factor in the cost of food, and as the cost of labour rises, so does the cost of food.

There are 650 constituencies in the UK; the House of Commons is 650 members strong. That means one seat per constituency. Each seat is represented by one MP.

MPs are elected for a five-year term, although a General Election can be called earlier, as in 2010. The House of Commons is not a permanent body.

We are bound by the rules of the House, but we are not bound to toe the party line. The role of the MP is to represent the interests of their constituents. We cannot vote in the interests of one group over another. Our primary concern is to be the best representatives of all our constituents.

MPs work long hours for little pay. The average MP earns just under £65,000 per year, compared to a cabinet minister’s salary of £139,000 per year. The average MP has to work 50 hours a week, compared to a cabinet minister’s 36 hours a week.

The job is not all about politics and campaigning; it is also about community service and public service. We have to be able to put the needs of the community first. We have to be able to put the needs of the community above our own personal interests.

The role of an MP is to be an advocate for the people who elect them, not the party that elected them. We have to be able to represent the people of our constituency, not just the people who voted for us.

The European Union is our only other neighbour. That is a fact that must be dealt with in the context of the border.

There are people who have been telling us that the problem is the common travel area. It is not. It is the border that is the problem. The second issue concerns the single market, which is something that we want and that the UK Government said it wanted. I do not believe that the UK Government has changed its mind on that. However, there is some confusion. I think that the confusion arises from the Government’s inability to understand that there is no such thing as a single market outside the European Union. It is not a separate entity to which we can have access. It is part of the European Union and it is not possible to have access to the single market unless we are part of the European Union.

In other words, the UK is currently part of the European Union single market. We are part of the European Union and we benefit from being part of the single market. That means that we are able to sell our goods and services to other parts of the European Union on the same terms as other parts of the European Union. That is a good thing and I want to continue to enjoy the benefits of the single market.

## South Yorkshire and Bassetlaw

The key objective of Rebuilding Ireland is to significantly increase the supply of homes to meet the needs of the population. In order to achieve this objective, there is a need to ensure there is sufficient supply of serviced land to support housing supply.

To this end, the Department of Housing, Planning and Local Government in collaboration with the Department of Arts, Heritage, Regional, Rural and Gaeltacht Affairs and the Local Government Management Agency is developing a framework to help facilitate the identification and development of land that could be made available for housing.

The framework, which was launched on 15th November, will be known as the “National Spatial Strategy Housing Infrastructure Delivery Framework”.

The framework is being developed in two phases:

- Phase 1 - The development of a National Strategic Infrastructure Model to identify a potential pipeline of land across the State with the aim of providing additional housing delivery capacity.
- Phase 2 - The development of an implementation framework to support the delivery of infrastructure and housing in line with the capacity identified in phase 1.

The framework is being developed in consultation with key stakeholders, including Local Authorities, and is intended to help identify land that could be made available for housing and help identify the infrastructure requirements to enable this land to be made available.

The framework will be completed by the end of 2017 and will be of value to Local Authorities in particular who are looking to identify potential land and infrastructure requirements for housing.

As part of the federal government’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the government made the decision to waive its quarantine requirements for temporary foreign workers in the meat processing sector. The government has said that this will allow meat processing facilities to bring in more workers from other countries to help meet the needs of the industry.

While we agree that this is an essential service and must continue, we do have concerns with this decision.

Our biggest concern is how temporary foreign workers are treated in Canada. Their working conditions, their ability to access basic services, and their ability to social distance are very concerning. We are concerned that the workers will be exposed to COVID-19 through this decision.

While we agree that this decision was made to ensure that our meat processing facilities can continue to operate, we have concerns about the conditions these workers are being subject to in Canada. We believe that they should be treated like any other worker, and that they should have the same rights and protections as Canadian workers.

We believe that the government should do more to protect the health and safety of these workers. We also believe that the government should do more to protect the health and safety of Canadians.

We know that the government has taken some steps to address this issue, but we believe that more needs to be done. We are calling on the government to:

The Liberal Party of Canada proposes that we auction off the spectrum licenses, but then put in place an obligation on the telcos to offer to sell off the spectrum to competitors at a fixed cost. For example, let’s say we auction off a 10 MHz band of spectrum and the telcos are bidding up to $4.5 billion. The telcos then win the auction and are then obligated to offer up that same 10 MHz band of spectrum to competitors at $400 million. If you’re a competitor and you want that spectrum, you can then buy it off the telco at that fixed price.

This is a simple and effective way to ensure that the competitive marketplace we have in Canada is protected and that Canadians aren’t paying a high price. It’s also a simple and effective way to ensure that the telcos don’t pay exorbitant prices for spectrum, prices that would eventually be passed on to the consumer.

At present the law makes an exception for workers, which means they are not included in the usual collective insolvency process, and as a result they are treated worse than everyone else.

The government should therefore amend the Insolvency Act 1986 to introduce a new collective insolvency procedure that is the same for workers as it is for everyone else.

That would mean that in the case of an insolvency, workers would be treated as general unsecured creditors and as a result would have to vote in support of a proposed Company Voluntary Arrangement (CVA) in order for it to come into force.

If the CVA was not approved, then the company would be put into compulsory liquidation, where workers would have the same rights as any other unsecured creditor to receive a dividend from the liquidator.

The legislation should also be changed to allow for workers to be treated as a class in insolvency proceedings. That would mean that in the case of an insolvency, workers would be able to vote for a liquidator or administrator to deal with the company’s affairs.

Finally, the legislation should be changed to allow workers to vote for a provisional liquidator in the case of a CVA being proposed.

I have made it clear that I would not support a subsidised nuclear power scheme that was more expensive than conventional fossil fuel generation.

The Government has set a target of generating 15 per cent of energy from renewable sources by 2020, and this target has been incorporated in the Climate Change Bill.

I believe that, in order to meet our emissions targets, we will have to invest in low-carbon energy generation, and that is why I have said that I would support nuclear power as one option to generate low-carbon electricity.

I have been advised by analysts that the most expensive way of generating low-carbon electricity is through nuclear, and the cheapest is through off-shore wind. I have therefore set a test that, for nuclear to be subsidised, it would have to be more cost-effective than off-shore wind.

The bill proposes amending the Criminal Code to strike out section 258 which allows for a warrantless search of a person's property under certain circumstances. I will explain the circumstances shortly.

The bill would strike out section 258 and replace it with a new section. The new section would allow a peace officer to search a person's vehicle, vessel, aircraft, or other conveyance when there are reasonable grounds to believe that the conveyance is being used in the commission of, or for the purpose of committing, an offence under the Criminal Code or under an act of Parliament that authorizes the peace officer to search for, seize, and confiscate the conveyance.

A peace officer would be allowed to search the conveyance without a warrant and could arrest the person if he found evidence of the offence. The peace officer would be allowed to seize any evidence of the offence and the conveyance.

The bill would also amend section 497.01 of the Criminal Code, which deals with the seizure and forfeiture of vehicles and other conveyances used in the commission of certain offences. Under this section, the Crown would have to bring the matter before a judge for a hearing. The judge would be allowed to order that the conveyance be seized, forfeited, and destroyed if there was reasonable evidence to believe that the conveyance was used in the commission of the offence.

Finally, the bill would amend the Criminal Code to allow the Crown to appeal to the court of appeal if the judge's ruling was not in its favour.

The armed forces covenant is the UK’s commitment to ensuring that those who serve or have served in the armed forces, and their families, are treated fairly. It recognises that the whole nation has a moral obligation to members of the armed forces and their families, and it establishes how they should expect to be treated.

The armed forces covenant is an enduring commitment. In July 2011, the Prime Minister made a commitment that the armed forces covenant will be “a living document, regularly reviewed and improved”. The commitment is backed by a cross-Government delivery board, which is chaired by the Minister for Defence People and Veterans, my right hon. Friend the Member for North East Somerset (Dr Murrison). The delivery board meets regularly to consider the covenant and how to improve the armed forces covenant.

The report has been prepared following the fourth annual review of the armed forces covenant, which took place earlier this year. The fourth annual report sets out progress made since the third annual review of the armed forces covenant in March 2015, and provides a comprehensive update of the implementation of the armed forces covenant and of the cross-Government workstreams. It also includes recommendations for future development. I am pleased to report that 414 individual actions have been implemented since the previous report was published in March 2015.

The report also includes an update on the workstreams agreed by the delivery board. a lecture on the Holocaust.

Auschwitz is the most famous extermination camp, but it was not the only one. The Nazis established more than 40,000 camps across Europe. Some of these were concentration camps where prisoners worked, others were prisons, and the most horrible were death camps, which were established in 1941.

These camps were where the Nazis developed their “Final Solution” of exterminating the Jews of Europe. They selected these camps based on their geographical location, proximity to transportation, availability of workers, and the presence of existing gas chambers and crematoria.

Of these camps, Auschwitz was the largest, housing over 1.1 million people, with 405,000 deaths. Treblinka was the most efficient, housing over 850,000 people, with 782,000 deaths. Sobibor was the most deadly, housing 250,000 people, with 250,000 deaths. Chelmno was the most secretive, housing 322,000 people, with 152,000 deaths.

When the Nazis invaded Poland, they imprisoned the country’s Jews in ghettos. These ghettos were like overcrowded cities where the Jews were forced to live in extreme poverty. The Nazis forced the Jews to work in factories and farms, and used them as slave labor.

Peatlands are the main natural carbon store in Europe. These spongy habitats of Sphagnum mosses and other plants and animals have been the main carbon sinks on earth, storing carbon in the form of peat, but they are also under serious pressure. The carbon sink is under threat from drainage, agricultural and forestry practices, which reduce the volume of peat and cause its degradation. As peatlands are not only threatened by the climate crisis, but also are part of the solution to the climate crisis, the EU has identified peatlands as a priority habitat.

According to Minister of State Hildegarde Naughton, “increased funding to €14 million will enable the restoration of 2,500 hectares of protected raised bogs across the midlands and will contribute to long-term carbon storage. I have no doubt that this funding will help to protect and restore peatlands, which store vast amounts of carbon”.

The restored peatlands will help to prevent erosion, increase biodiversity, protect water quality and will help to mitigate the impact of climate change. The funds are being distributed to 50 projects through the new Midlands Peatlands Restoration Levy (MPRL), which was introduced in 2019 as part of the Climate Action Plan 2019. The 50 projects will be delivered over five years by the National Parks and Wildlife Service and the landowners will receive 50% of the project cost.

We are in the midst of a pandemic. People are losing jobs and livelihoods. The economic fallout from COVID-19 will be felt for years to come. Canadians are counting on their leaders to work together for the good of the country.

So it was unfortunate to see Conservative leader Andrew Scheer attack Prime Minister Justin Trudeau for the way the government has handled the COVID-19 response. In a statement on April 28, Scheer questioned the Trudeau government’s decision to provide $52.5 billion in financial support to businesses and workers, saying it had been a “massive waste of taxpayer money.”

Scheer went on to say that the Prime Minister was “out of touch” and “unaccountable” for spending $817 million on advertising to promote his government’s response to the pandemic.

Scheer’s comments were just the latest in a series of snipes directed at the PM and it is difficult not to see the political gamesmanship involved. The purpose of the Bill is to give effect to the United Nations convention on the rights of persons with disabilities. It is a human rights instrument that has been adopted by 157 states, including the UK, and has been signed by 149 states. The convention is the first comprehensive human rights treaty of its kind, covering all aspects of life for people with disabilities.

The UK is committed to the principles of the convention. The Government have already taken steps to give effect to the convention in this country. In June, the UK became the first country in the world to ratify the convention. The Bill, which we have introduced today, will complete the implementation process.

The Bill provides a coherent framework to give effect to the convention, which has been welcomed by leading organisations representing people with disabilities. The Bill brings together and clarifies our obligations under the convention and ensures that disabled people have the legal protection that they need, and that disabled people’s rights are enshrined in law, and are promoted and protected in practice.
