A woman’s menstrual cycle is a monthly reminder that her body is in sync with the seasons. The changing length of daylight affects the brain’s production of the hormones estrogen and progesterone. And a woman’s menstrual cycle, in turn, affects the balance of these hormones. When estrogen and progesterone are balanced, a woman feels good. The production of these hormones declines as she ages. After menopause, her menstrual cycle ends. And so ends the natural balance of her hormones.

## Why do women’s bodies need hormones?

Hormones are the body’s chemical messengers. They act as a link between our bodies’ systems to help maintain homeostasis. Homeostasis is a natural biological mechanism in which the body is able to regulate its internal environment in order to maintain optimal conditions. Hormones are secreted by the glands into the bloodstream where they travel to their target organs, tissues, or cells.

## What are the hormones in women’s bodies?

There are three types of hormones. Steroid hormones are produced by the ovaries. They are responsible for sexual development and fertility. The pituitary gland releases hormones that stimulate growth and metabolism. The thyroid gland produces thyroid hormones that control the rate at which the body uses energy, makes proteins, and controls the use of other hormones.

Now that restrictions are easing and our lives are returning to some semblance of normality, we look forward to the hope and the light of summer.

In the darkness, we remember the words of a poem by William Cowper:

God moves in a mysterious way
His wonders to perform,
He plants His footsteps in the sea
And rides upon the storm.

Dark the night! Clouds and tempests,
Still He holds me close;
In the chaos and confusion
God's love surrounds my soul.

Yes, His light and love and mercy
Are ever near me.
In the darkness of my fears,
God's love enfolded me.

As the storms of life come and go
I know my Rock is He.
He is Lord of heaven and earth,
Lord of the stormy sea.

As we enter into the light of summer, may we always remember the darkness of that dark night and may we be always grateful for the light and the love and mercy of our God.

Tony Walsh

On Wednesday, 24 January 2018, the United Kingdom Parliament enacted the European Union (Withdrawal) Bill 2017-2019. The bill, which grants the UK Government powers to disapply EU law and amend or repeal legislation without the consent of Parliament, passed in the House of Commons by 326 votes to 290. The Bill received Royal Assent on 26 June 2018.

The European Union (Withdrawal) Bill 2017-2019 allows the United Kingdom Government to repeal the European Communities Act 1972, which incorporates the law of the European Union into the domestic law of the UK. It also allows the UK Government to disapply EU law in UK courts, even though it is still in force in the EU.

The bill was introduced to Parliament in July 2017 by David Davis, the Secretary of State for Exiting the European Union, following the European Union (Notification of Withdrawal) Act 2017, which was passed by Parliament on 16 March 2017. It is one of the most important pieces of legislation to be passed in the UK since the European Communities Act 1972, and is a key part of the United Kingdom’s ‘Great Repeal Bill.’

I want to quote from a paper entitled “The Debt Burden”. I would like to go back to the point that I was making earlier, that the debt burden is not just in terms of the money. What is really important is the effect it has on future generations.

As I have said, I am a parent. I have two children. I am very concerned about what this generation of Canadians is doing to the future of our country. In fact, we could call it the “debt burden”.

The debt burden is not just in terms of the money. The debt burden is also about what it will mean for future generations.

Canadians are facing an unprecedented financial crisis. The federal debt is more than $400 billion, and it is growing by $5 billion each and every month. This debt is a serious concern to all Canadians. It is a serious concern to all Canadians because it means that money that could be used to invest in our future is being used to pay interest on the debt.

We have already passed the point of no return. We are at a critical stage. The financial crisis we are facing is the worst in our history. In fact, we are borrowing more money today than at any other time in our history.

If we do not get our finances under control, we will not be able to pay for the programs and services that we need. We will not be able to pay for the infrastructure that we need to make our communities stronger. We will not be able to pay for the education that our children need to succeed in the future.

What is really important is that Canadians understand that this is not just about the money. This is also about what it means for the future of our country. We have to take action now to get our finances under control.

It was the first step on the long road towards full women’s suffrage in the UK, but there is still plenty to celebrate today.

The path to women’s suffrage was long and paved with struggle and setbacks. The early suffragists, such as Emmeline Pankhurst, fought for their right to vote, refusing to accept the idea that they were not full citizens. Their efforts led to the Representation of the People Act, and to the even more significant Representation of the People Act of 1928, which gave all women over the age of 21 the vote on equal terms with men.

The Women’s Institute is one of the largest women’s organisations in the UK, with members throughout the country. Today, on its 100th anniversary, the WI is celebrating the right to vote in its own special way.

The WI has been a voice for women since 1915, campaigning for votes for women, better working conditions and the right to be taken seriously. We are celebrating the centenary by encouraging women to get involved in the political process and to make their voices heard.

These are two very important issues which have not been included in the discussions on Brexit.

The European Arrest Warrant has been a very successful tool since it was introduced in 2004, and is an essential part of the EU’s cross-border police cooperation. It is used more than 8,000 times per year, and has resulted in the arrest of thousands of people suspected of serious crimes, such as murder, rape, child abuse, and people smuggling.

Since the Brexit vote, arrests and extraditions have dropped significantly, as many European countries are reluctant to issue arrest warrants for the UK because of the uncertainty of what will happen in 2019.

The Sirena system allows police and border control to quickly and effectively share information about foreign nationals, and will remain in place until at least 2020, but without an agreement on our future relationship with Europe there is no guarantee it will continue after that.

The Sirena system has been a huge success, and has helped to prevent 58,000 foreign criminals from entering the UK and has assisted in the deportation of more than 10,000 foreign criminals.

With the EU’s help, the UK has been able to stop 472 attempted terrorist attacks, and these systems have been essential to this success.

Despite the fact that Brexit will cause problems for these important systems, the Home Secretary has refused to take any action to address these issues.

The Home Secretary should be working to find a way to ensure the European Arrest Warrant continues to operate, but instead she is refusing to take any action to try and find a solution.

A recent report by the Irish Medicines Board showed that there are 103 medicinal products manufactured in Ireland, down from 160 in 2005. It also revealed that 36 companies have ceased manufacturing in Ireland in the past 10 years.

As the process has been undertaken, it has become more and more clear that the consultation process is inadequate for the effective implementation of these reserves.

While the Government and NGOs have been quick to point out that the establishment of the reserves is not about putting people out of work, the reality is that the consultation process is inadequate. The MPA process is not about consultation, it is about imposition. The Government has already decided that the establishment of these reserves is a non-negotiable item.

Therefore, the real issue becomes: How can we effectively implement these reserves without disrupting the livelihoods of affected operators? In the case of Bonaire, it is clear that this has been done. As a result, the island has had to re-invent itself in order to attract new visitors. Unfortunately, the re-invention of Bonaire has not been about protecting the livelihoods of current operators.

With this in mind, I see two main options for the establishment of the MPAs: 1) abandon the consultation process and implement reserves immediately; or 2) find a way to adequately include those who will be affected in the process of reserve establishment.

## 1) What is your opinion on the Climate Action Plan, and what is the best way to measure its success?

The Climate Action Plan is ambitious, but as we have seen with the budget, there are other challenges such as the housing crisis that have to be taken into account. There is a strong focus on renewable energy and on retrofitting buildings. The focus on retrofitting buildings is important as we are responsible for 27% of emissions, and this is the area where we can make the most difference. The plan is also focused on increasing biodiversity and the natural environment.

I think the most important thing for the success of the plan will be how we pay for it. Will it come out of the public purse, or will we be able to get funding from the EU?

## Finland supports the reform process

Finland has consistently supported the EU’s engagement and the reform process in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The EU has been the largest donor to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it is the biggest external trade partner of the country. We support Bosnia and Herzegovina’s efforts to implement the necessary reforms in order to move closer to the EU.

In May 2016, the EU presented a new strategy for Bosnia and Herzegovina. The strategy aims to strengthen the EU’s role in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to increase the efficiency of EU assistance, and to support the implementation of the EU-Bosnia and Herzegovina Sectoral Integration Reforms.

In the fall of 2016, the Liberals promised to make EI benefits more accessible and flexible, but what we have seen since is a broken promise. EI reforms that were put in place in 2006 have been stripped away. Workers have been left with less flexibility in their work options.

I was interested to hear the member for Winnipeg North talk about the number of people on EI benefits in his riding. Let us look at the facts. In the last fiscal year, there were 3,087 people on EI benefits in Winnipeg North. The year before, there were 2,363 people on EI benefits in Winnipeg North, so that number has gone up. The Liberals promised to help people get back to work. They promised to help people be more flexible, but they have done nothing.

In addition, the Liberals promised to make EI benefits more affordable, but once again they have failed. Since the Liberals came to power, the EI premium has increased by 43%. It is now $1.61 a week for the average worker. That is a huge increase. In the last five years, the EI premium has increased by more than 66%. The Liberals promised to make EI benefits more affordable, but once again they have failed.

The Liberals have failed to fix EI. They have failed to make EI benefits more flexible or more affordable. They have failed to deliver for Canadians. Canadians are paying for the government's mistakes.

The Government of Canada is proud of its tradition of celebrating Canada's multiculturalism and of encouraging Canadians to celebrate the heritage of their family's country of origin or ethnicity. In addition to our annual celebration of Canada Day, Canadians celebrate a variety of other events that are important to them. These events include celebrations of St. Patrick's Day, St. Jean Baptiste Day, Diwali, the Day of Mourning, Thanksgiving, and others.

The Government of Canada is not in the business of choosing which celebrations are worthy of support and which are not. However, given the resources available to the government and the number of celebrations that occur throughout the year, it is simply not possible to provide funding for all of them.

As you may know, the Government of Canada has a policy of providing funding for events that are organized by a not-for-profit organization. The Government of Canada has also supported the celebrations of Canada's multiculturalism by providing a contribution to the Multiculturalism Program, which is administered by the Department of Canadian Heritage. This program includes a component that provides funding for community-based projects and activities that help newcomers adapt and become full participants in Canadian society.

I encourage you to continue to celebrate your cultural heritage as you see fit, and I thank you for taking the time to share your thoughts on this issue with me.

Conservative Members have welcomed the Malthouse compromise. Can my right hon. Friend assure me that he has not yet accepted the notion of a second referendum, and that he has not accepted any form of the customs union?

My hon. Friend has a very valid point. The Malthouse compromise is being discussed by the Government, and we are trying to work out whether it could actually work. As I have said, I have some doubts about that, but we shall see whether that idea can be developed into a workable solution. It is no good having an idea that sounds good, but which is not workable.

If the Malthouse compromise is workable, and if we are able to get a deal, it must include no backstop. As I have said in this Chamber before, I think that the backstop as it currently stands would be a very bad deal for the United Kingdom, and I am sure that my right hon. Friend agrees. It would effectively mean that we would have to keep abiding by all the regulations of the EU, yet without having any say in them. That would be very bad for the United Kingdom.

As I have said before, I think that the EEA/EFTA model is the one to go for. I know that there are some on the Government Benches who do not agree with that, but if there is a way of moving in that direction, I think it is something that we should be looking at. I do not think that the deal that is currently on the table is the one that we should be going for, or that we would be very well served by.

Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) adheres to the principles of good governance by providing parliamentarians with access to the information they need to be effective and to hold the government accountable.

This is a long-standing demand of the Canada Border Services Agency Committee. In the last Parliament, the CBSA Committee called on the government to provide annual reports to Parliament. The government has agreed with that recommendation and is tabling this legislation.

The legislation also provides for the Canada Border Services Agency Committee to call on the CBSA to provide reports on specific subjects. This gives the Committee the tools it needs to be effective.

The bill would also give the Canada Border Services Agency Committee the power to conduct studies on subjects of interest to Parliament. This would be an important tool to help the Committee fulfill its duties.

The bill would also give the Canada Border Services Agency Committee the power to ask the CBSA to provide information and documents for the purposes of its work.

The legislation would also establish a CBSA Ombudsman. This new position will be responsible for receiving and reviewing complaints from the public about the CBSA. This would be an important role for the CBSA Ombudsman to ensure that the CBSA is accountable to the Canadian public.

I would like to thank the CBSA Committee for its hard work on this legislation. I would also like to thank the government for its support for this important bill.

#### What the 2018 Budget has to offer

In his Budget 2018 speech, the Minister for Public Expenditure & Reform, Paschal Donohoe TD, said: “I am now in a position to announce the terms of the Lansdowne Road Agreement for new entrants to the public service.”

The measures will be contained in legislation which will be published in the coming weeks. They will be in effect for the 2018 pay round and will apply to those public servants who started work on or after 1 October 2015.

The measures will be in place until the end of the year, when the current Lansdowne Road Agreement will end. It is expected that a successor agreement will be reached between the Government and the trade unions before this date.

#### What are the new pay measures?

The new measures will:

- Introduce a 10% pay progression for new entrants to the public service over three years to bring their pay up to €29,656. This will be in effect from 1 January 2018
- Increase the minimum entry point for public service staff on the single scale to €27,500 from 1 January 2018 and to €29,656 by 1 January 2020.

It was the same with Chaucer. I was taught to read his Canterbury Tales and to pronounce them aloud in a rather high, schoolboy fashion, so that I never really got the measure of them. I knew that there was a lot of fun, and some very funny people, and that there was also a great deal of ribaldry, but I did not really appreciate the humour, nor did I feel very much sympathy with Chaucer’s characters, who seemed to be very remote from me. I thought they were old-fashioned, out of touch with my own time, and I did not find the stories very gripping. I suppose this was because I could not see myself in them, and I felt no special identification.

At that time, and perhaps still, there was the idea that to enjoy the Canterbury Tales you had to be a schoolboy, and I was not a schoolboy. I found them rather remote and alien.

This changed when I was 27 years old and first became seriously interested in writing. I discovered that the stories were not just old-fashioned, they were not just amusing, or ribald, or funny, or didactic. They were also the source of a new kind of writing.

In my early 20s, I had read Samuel Butler’s The Way of All Flesh, and I had also been interested in what was then called ‘realism’, which meant the attempt to write about the real world in a way which was neither romantic nor idealistic. The way to do this, it seemed to me, was to write in a plain, factual way, using ordinary language, and not attempting to dress things up with poetic or rhetorical language.

This had the effect of bringing my writing nearer to the way I spoke,

1. The Covid-19 pandemic is not just an IT problem. While technology is part of the solution, the primary problem we need to solve is that the virus is spreading in our community. 2. We need a team that can work cross-functionally to manage all parts of the contact tracing process. This includes the team of contact tracers that will actually reach out to people who test positive, and to those they may have been in contact with. This will also require working with the IT team to build the systems necessary for the contact tracing to work, and with the medical and nursing staff to do the testing.
3. Covid-19 is not the only disease out there, and the Public Health team are working on tackling other diseases too. There are a number of other diseases that are of concern, such as the measles and monkeypox, which are both airborne and can be spread between humans. The team needs to be able to handle both at the same time, and the skills required for these diseases are broadly the same.
4. There is an inherent conflict between the goal of Covid-19 testing and tracing and the goal of protecting people from other diseases. In order to stop Covid-19, we need to be able to test people who have the virus, and we need to be able to do that quickly and efficiently. However, we also need to be able to protect people from other diseases, and in some cases, this means limiting testing so that we don’t spread the disease further. The Public Health team is the best placed to make this decision.

It is a very important question: do unborn children have rights? They certainly have rights in the womb. Do they have rights once they are born? It is a very difficult question to answer. It is a question that I wrestled with as a young man when I was a minister in the Howard government. I had to consider whether to support a bill of an independent senator, a Mr Fielding, to support the rights of unborn children. I thought long and hard about it, and eventually decided to support the bill.

As I say, it is a difficult question. I will give a little bit of my personal story. When I was 16 I had a girlfriend and we were going steady. We decided that we were going to get married when we were 17, so we got a marriage licence. She became pregnant. I was 16. It was not a happy time. It was a bit of a shock. We were young, immature and unsure of what to do. So we made a decision that we were going to terminate the pregnancy. I was 16 years old.

It is a difficult question to answer. My story is not unique. There are many people in this place who have had the same experience, both sides of the House. It is a difficult question. I am not a theologian, I am not a philosopher, but I do know that I have been where many people in this place have been. I have had to wrestle with the question. In the end, I have decided that, if an unborn child has rights, then surely that child's rights must be balanced against the rights of the mother and the father.

Some years there might be a few names on the list, other years none. On one occasion the principal noticed that there were no children in my class who were in need of referral. He was surprised and asked me how I managed it.

I told him that I had never had a child in my class that I thought needed referral. I explained that it wasn’t because I thought any of my pupils were perfect. It was because I made a point of spending the first few weeks of the new school year getting to know the pupils, understanding their backgrounds and their family circumstances. I also tried to find out how they felt about the school, if they enjoyed coming to school, and whether they had any worries or concerns.

By the time I was ready to refer a child, I had already referred him or her to the school counsellor or to me. I explained to the principal that I used my knowledge of the children to try and anticipate their needs. I found that if I could identify a child who was having difficulties, I could deal with them sooner, before they developed more serious problems.

I was surprised to hear that no one else had ever thought to do this, but I have since discovered that the vast majority of teachers are completely unaware of how important this aspect of their work is. I have met many teachers who have told me that they have children who have been with them for years, and they are still unaware of what is happening in the children’s lives.

What is even more surprising is that there are very few supports available to teachers to help them get to know their pupils. Teachers are encouraged to adopt a more ‘business-like’ approach to their work. The emphasis is on achieving targets, on delivering the curriculum, and on dealing with behavioural issues. This means that teachers do not have much time to get to know their pupils.

In my recent article on this site I outlined some of the problems that have been created by our failure to update our social security system and labour market regulation in line with changes to the world of work.

The economic response to Covid-19 has been unprecedented, and although it is welcome, it also demonstrates the scale of the problems.

The furlough scheme is an emergency measure to protect jobs. It has been necessary to introduce it in the context of the emergency, and I welcome it as a temporary measure to prevent businesses going under and people being put on the dole.

The emergency measures to support people who have lost their jobs or been put on reduced hours are similarly welcome, as is the provision to help pay the rent, and I hope the government will consider further measures to support self-employed people who do not pay themselves wages or to help pay household bills.

We need to learn from this experience to inform a long-term plan for social security and work to create a labour market that is fairer and more productive.

We need a social security system that protects people from the worst effects of an economic crisis without condemning them to a life on benefits.

We need a labour market that is fair to everyone who wants to work, whether they are employed or self-employed, whether they have a fixed or zero-hour contract, and whether they are paid the minimum wage or more.

We need social security that is flexible and responsive to changes in the world of work, and we need employment laws that enable people to balance work and family responsibilities, and we need to recognise the importance of good working conditions for economic growth and for the wellbeing of people at work.

The Bill clarifies the criteria for the Rental Pressure Zone designation. This designation takes into account the number of persons in a household per dwelling and the housing demand and supply of the area. It also takes into account the number of persons per dwelling for the entire RPZ.

The Bill ensures that landlords can still apply to the Residential Tenancies Board to have a tenancy order amended, if they can demonstrate that a tenant is in breach of a term of a tenancy agreement. ### Written Answers — Department for Education: Higher Education (16 Jul 2018)

Chris Green: To ask the Secretary of State for Education, with reference to the letter to Professor Sir Adrian Smith dated 24 January 2018, what assessment he has made of the impact of the removal of student maintenance grants on the ability of higher education institutions to recruit and support students; and if he will make a statement.

Damian Hinds: The Government’s student support package continues to be one of the most generous in the world. All new full-time students in the UK can access a package of financial support that covers the costs of living, tuition fees and loans for living costs. There are no up-front costs for tuition fees for students from the UK and EU, and all students can choose to defer repayment of their student loan until they are earning above a set threshold. For the 2017-18 academic year, the repayment threshold was £21,000, and will be £25,000 from April 2018.

I begin my remarks, I want to acknowledge that I am speaking to you today from the traditional territory of the Algonquin Anishinaabe people.

For far too long, indigenous women and girls have been victims of unspeakable violence, and far too many of them have gone missing or have been murdered. For far too long, their families have been left to wonder what happened to their loved ones. For far too long, our justice system has failed to uphold the rights of indigenous women and girls and to protect them from violent offenders.

Far too many indigenous women have been killed or gone missing without anyone being held accountable. This must end, and it must end now.

As we have heard from all speakers today, the government is committed to addressing the issue of missing and murdered indigenous women and girls. However, the government has yet to develop a national action plan to address this crisis.

In fact, it is hard to imagine that the government is serious about addressing the issue when it is taking so long to do so. It has been almost two years since the Prime Minister promised to develop a national action plan.

During that time, more than 30 women and girls have gone missing or have been murdered. We cannot continue to wait. We cannot continue to let families wonder what happened to their loved ones. We cannot continue to let violent offenders go free. We cannot continue to let the government do the bare minimum and expect the families of the missing and murdered indigenous women and girls to be satisfied.

In the House of Commons, there have been debates, there have been resolutions, and there have been votes, but we have yet to see a national action plan from this government.

I have spoken about the missing and murdered indigenous women and girls issue in this House before, and I will continue to do so until a national action plan is developed.

I know the Holocaust was a painful time in history for Jews and for many others, including people of other faiths. The Holocaust was a painful time in history for me, too, and I am not Jewish.

The Holocaust is so important in Jewish history that many Jews are named after the event: Yadidah (God’s gift), Yisroel (God rules), Malkah (queen), Malkiel (God is king), Yisrael (God rules), Shimon (God has heard), Shlomo (peace) and many others.

The Holocaust is so important in Jewish history that many of us have a special place in our hearts and our homes for a menorah, a holiday candle holder that symbolizes the miracle of Hanukkah.

The Holocaust is so important in Jewish history that we are proud of our tradition and celebrate the Torah and its teachings and the role of the Torah in the history of the Jewish people.

The Holocaust is so important in Jewish history that we are proud of our culture and celebrate our Jewish identity and celebrate our Jewish culture.

The Holocaust is so important in Jewish history that we celebrate Jewish holidays, including Hanukkah, Purim, Sukkot, Yom Kippur and Rosh Hashanah.

## NHS Continuing Healthcare

### Question

To ask Her Majesty’s Government how much funding was allocated for NHS continuing healthcare in the financial year 2016–17; and how much of that amount was spent on NHS continuing healthcare. [HL249]

The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Health (Lord O’Shaughnessy): NHS continuing healthcare (CHC) is a package of care arranged and funded solely by the NHS for individuals who have been assessed as having a primary health need. NHS continuing healthcare is free to eligible individuals, whether that care is provided in a hospital, hospice or care home.

In 2016-17, £3.3 billion was allocated to continuing healthcare.

I am pleased that the report confirms that Select Committees remain a vital part of the parliamentary process, and that they are entitled to receive full and prompt compliance with their requests for evidence. It is also right that the report sets out that the powers of Select Committees should be exercised judiciously, as the report makes clear, and with due regard to the interests of those who provide evidence.

As the report notes, the current system of Select Committee procedure is governed by the House’s ancient privileges. The report acknowledges that, since 1979, the House has used its privileges to clarify and strengthen the powers of Select Committees, and to lay down rules about the conduct of Committee proceedings. The report sets out recommendations to bring the privileges into the 21st century, including to require Select Committees to publish the reasons for their summonses and to allow the Committees to summon witnesses from outside this country.

The report also makes recommendations to strengthen the system of parliamentary privilege, including to allow witnesses to claim privilege in the courts in the same way as parliamentarians. I am grateful to the report for making those recommendations.

The Government are grateful to the Committee for its work and look forward to discussing these important issues with the Committee further, in due course.

## The problem

Rents are rising and so is the cost of living. The number of renters in the UK has increased from 2.4 million in 1981 to 4.6 million in 2013 – that’s one in five households now renting privately. And for many people, renting has become a permanent, rather than a temporary, way of life.

Too many people are stuck in a system with no power to challenge rogue landlords and no savings to get on the housing ladder.

Renters need a deal that gives them the security and rights they need.

## Our solution

- We want to see the UK Government introducing a Renters’ Deal, with a specific focus on helping young people. This would include the following:
- Renters’ Right to Buy, so that renters can own their home at a discounted price
- Renters’ Right to Save, so that renters can save for a mortgage deposit
- Renters’ Right to Switch, so that renters can move easily between properties and landlords

The court can also decide that the parole order should continue and the person should be returned to prison but should be released again on parole. The third course of action is that the court can decide that the parole order should continue and the person should be returned to prison, but should be released on licence. It is to stop the current situation, where a man and a woman who are married can be living together in the same house, and, when they decide to split up, one partner decides to sell the house and the other partner has to leave and go into rented accommodation. There is not even the possibility of buying the house at market value, because the person who owns the house has a right to sell it to somebody else. I have heard many, many stories of this happening in cases where a man and a woman have been living together. When they decide to split up, the man moves out and sells the house, so that the woman has no option but to buy a property or move into rented accommodation.

When a couple get married, they have a right to buy their house. What I am trying to do is ensure that a man and a woman who live together have the same rights as a man and a woman who are married. The same applies to couples of the same sex who have been living together for a year or more. The Bill is about granting rights to people who have made a long-term commitment to each other and who have a house together.

I know that many people will not agree with me and that there is much discussion about the morality of people who live together rather than getting married. - allows victims to apply to the Court of Appeal for leave to appeal a sentence that has been imposed by a Provincial Court judge in cases of sexual assault;

As well as the physical health of people with diabetes, there is also a huge mental health aspect to it. A diabetes diagnosis can have a devastating effect on people’s mental health, and the NHS has a duty to make sure that the mental health support is there for people with diabetes when they need it.

Many people living with diabetes, particularly those who are dependent on insulin, find that the stress of dealing with the condition can have a negative impact on their mental health. Many people who have diabetes also have other conditions that can affect their mental health, such as depression and anxiety. Those things can lead to feelings of isolation, and feelings of isolation can lead to further mental health issues. The stress of having to regularly inject oneself with insulin can have a negative effect on one’s mental health.

A study by the charity Diabetes UK in 2017 found that 50% of people with diabetes said they had experienced at least one episode of depression during their life, compared with 30% of people without diabetes. The study also found that 56% of people with diabetes said that it made them feel sad, while 52% said that it made them feel anxious.

It is also worth mentioning the issue of diabetes and eating disorders, which can be particularly common among young people with type 1 diabetes. The mental health impact of diabetes can be very serious, and it is something that we must take seriously and work to address.

## Managing mental health with diabetes

Diabetes is a chronic disease that requires lifelong management. It can be a challenging condition to live with, both physically and mentally. Our children with speech and language disorders have the same potential as all children, and they deserve the chance to reach it.

In that case, a group of former employees of Barclays Bank had been employed under fixed term contracts. They were all made redundant by Barclays in June 2014. Before making those redundancies, Barclays had made a number of other redundancies, which meant that the number of workers who were made redundant in June 2014 was less than 20. The employees claimed that the redundancies which occurred before June 2014 should be counted towards the total, meaning that the redundancies in June 2014 could not be considered collective redundancies.

This was a major concession to the DUP, as it represented a reversal of the UK’s position, which had been that Northern Ireland, like the rest of the UK, should remain part of the single market and customs union. The British government had also been keen to retain Northern Ireland’s participation in the EU’s Common Travel Area, which allowed British and Irish citizens to travel freely between the two countries.

The DUP’s insistence that Northern Ireland should be treated differently from the rest of the UK was a major obstacle to reaching a deal with the EU. The EU had been clear that it would not agree to any deal that would weaken the integrity of the single market and customs union. This left the UK government with little room to manoeuvre.

The UK government’s decision to trigger Article 50 on 29 March 2017 set in motion a two-year process that would culminate in the UK’s withdrawal from the EU on 29 March 2019. This created a sense of urgency in the negotiations, as both sides were keen to reach a deal before the deadline.

However, I want to highlight some other important things that we are doing. For example, the redistribution of electoral districts will be the first process conducted using the Fair Representation Act, which came into force in 2017. That act established rules to ensure that ridings have similar populations and that new ridings are created if a population change requires it. The act will be administered by the independent Electoral Boundaries Commission, whose members have been appointed.

The commission will review the population change that occurred from 2016 to 2020 and determine the population of each electoral district. It will then consider the communities of interest within the province, including where people have common interests or characteristics, and it will ensure that the electoral districts are compact, where possible. It will also make sure that each electoral district is named after an identifiable geographical area and that electoral districts do not cross time zones.

This process of redistribution is important because it will make sure that people's voices are represented in Parliament. We want to ensure that the electoral districts are reflective of the needs and wishes of the people of Alberta.

We are also committed to working with the commission and making sure that there is transparency and openness in this process. If you are a homeowner looking for a builder, there are some simple steps to take that can help you find the right one for you.

Step 1 – Don’t believe the hype!

Be aware that rogue builders deliberately try to make themselves look good on the web and in the press. The internet is an easy target for rogues because they can create a web page that looks good, but which is not based on any facts. I know one rogue builder who has a huge list of testimonials on his web page. When I investigated them, I found that they were all faked, having been taken from the web pages of other builders.

Step 2 – Look for a builder who belongs to a trade body

There are many different trade bodies in the UK. Some are very well known, such as the Federation of Master Builders. Others are less well known, such as the National Federation of Builders and the Federation of Master Builders Scotland. You can find a list of all the major trade bodies, along with details of what they do, here.

The benefit of using a builder who belongs to a trade body is that they are held to certain standards. The main trade bodies have systems in place to help you find a reliable builder, and you can also use them to check if a builder belongs to a trade body before you use them.

Step 3 – Ask questions and get answers

Ask lots of questions. How long have they been in business? How many employees do they have? Do they have public liability insurance? Do they have employer’s liability insurance? Have they ever been sued, and if so, what was the outcome?

The answers to these questions will give you some idea of the type of builder you are dealing
